newsitem.title: LIBERIA: West Africa ministers set May 30 for Liberia polls.
newsitem.headline: West Africa ministers set May 30 for Liberia polls.

text.p: West African foreign ministers said on Friday that Liberia would hold presidential and parliamentary election on May 30 to end seven years of civil war.

The ministers, from a committee of nine states overseeing the peace process in the shattered West African nation, confirmed the date after a two-day meeting at a conference centre outside the capital Monrovia.

"I'd like to confirm that there will be elections to install a democratically-elected parliament, that is an assembly, and also a president with his vice-president on May 30, 1997," Nigerian Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi told a news conference.

Ikimi, chairman of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) committee, said the commander of the Nigerian-led ECOWAS peacekeeping force was satisfied on the security front following the disarmament of faction fighters.

General Victor Malu, he said, had reported "the successful conclusion of the disarmament and demobilisation exercise and that there were enough security guarantees to go ahead with the implementation of the entire Abuja accord as planned."

The peace accord, agreed in Nigeria's capital last August, followed a dozen collapsed deals in the nation that was formed in 1847 by freed American slaves and has retained close emotional links with the United States.

U.S. helicopters airlifted out U.S. and other foreign nationals during a flare-up in the war in Monrovia last April and May. They are now due to bring in extra West African peacekeeping troops over the next few days to bolster the peace process.
Faction leader Charles Taylor, who launched the war from Ivory Coast in December 1989, has already announced plans to stand for president. So has Alhaji Kromah, his sometime rival and sometime ally.
Ikimi said the elections would be organised by an independent electoral commission grouping representatives of the warring factions, political parties and society at large.

Voting would be by proportional representation. "The proportional representation type of elections is necessary because the existing constituencies have been eroded by the seven years of civil war," he said.

Ikimi also said there would be no voting outside Liberia -- a contentious issue since hundreds of thousands of Liberians are camped in neighbouring countries, mainly Ivory Coast. "The refugees will be repatriated home to take part in the voting," he said.

He gave no details on whether, when or how a census of voters would be held, but he said a new supreme court would be formed with ECOWAS ensuring that it was truly impartial. The court would check the election results and rulie on any disputes.
Well over 150,000 people, many of them civilians, have been killed in the civil war.
